metadata.research_scope: Clinical trials, safety profiles, mechanisms of action, pharmacopeia status (2020-2026)
metadata.sources_note: Data compiled from PubMed, PMC, WHO resources, WebMD, Drugs.com, Frontiers, ScienceDirect, and other peer-reviewed databases

latest_research.title: Tinospora Cordifolia (Giloy)-Induced Liver Injury During the COVID-19 Pandemic - Multicenter Nationwide Study From India
latest_research.finding: Retrospective study across 13 Indian centers identified 43 patients with herb-induced liver injury (HILI) temporally associated with Giloy use. Median time from initial consumption to symptom onset was 46 days. Presentations included acute hepatitis, acute worsening of chronic liver disease, and acute liver failure.

latest_research.title: Tinospora cordifolia (Giloy): An insight on the multifarious pharmacological paradigms of a most promising medicinal ayurvedic herb
latest_research.finding: Comprehensive review in Heliyon documenting diverse pharmacological activities including anti-diabetic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, hepatoprotective, and immunomodulatory properties attributed to alkaloids, diterpenoid lactones, glycosides, steroids, sesquiterpenoids, and phenolics.

latest_research.title: Genome sequencing and functional analysis of a multipurpose medicinal herb Tinospora cordifolia (Giloy)
latest_research.finding: First draft genome assembly of T. cordifolia produced using advanced sequencing technologies, comprising 1.01 Gbp. Functional analysis identified key biosynthetic gene clusters responsible for production of pharmacologically active metabolites.

latest_research.title: Integrated omics analysis of Tinospora cordifolia intervention in hypertriglyceridemia patients - pilot clinical trial
latest_research.finding: Pilot clinical trial demonstrated that T. cordifolia intervention modulated multiple signaling pathways in hypertriglyceridemia patients, providing multi-omics evidence for its lipid-lowering mechanisms.

latest_research.title: Giloy Ghanvati (Tinospora cordifolia) Reversed SARS-CoV-2 Viral Spike-Protein Induced Disease Phenotype in Humanized Zebrafish
latest_research.finding: Xenotransplant model study showed Giloy Ghanvati formulation reversed SARS-CoV-2 spike-protein induced disease phenotype, suggesting potential antiviral immunomodulatory activity.

latest_research.title: Exploring the Medicinal and Nutraceutical Frontiers of Tinospora cordifolia in Stress and Cancer Management
latest_research.finding: Review of T. cordifolia's ability to enhance antioxidant defenses and induce apoptosis in cancerous cells, with potential as adjunct therapy to improve quality of life for cancer patients.

safety_updates: Over 50 cases of clinically apparent acute liver injury reported since 2017, with increased incidence during the COVID-19 pandemic due to widespread self-medication
Multicenter Indian study (13 centers, 43 patients) confirmed association between Giloy use and herb-induced liver injury with autoimmune-like features
Major concern identified: botanical misidentification of Tinospora crispa (known hepatotoxin) being sold as T. cordifolia (Guduchi/Giloy) in Indian markets
LiverTox (NCBI) resource updated June 2025 with comprehensive hepatotoxicity data
Pharmacokinetic interactions reported with hypoglycemic drugs - aqueous extract may potentiate blood sugar lowering effects
Safe at concentrations up to 2000 mg/kg in short-term studies when authentic species is confirmed
Debate continues: some researchers argue hepatotoxicity reports are due to species adulteration rather than authentic T. cordifolia
mechanisms: Immunomodulation via activation of tumor-associated macrophages and increased IFN-gamma production
NF-kB pathway modulation and interleukin regulation for anti-inflammatory effects
Berberine (isoquinoline alkaloid) inhibits TNF-alpha-mediated proinflammatory pathways and suppresses iNOS activity to reduce nitrosative stress
Berberine targets multiple cell signaling pathways including proliferation, differentiation, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (anticancer)
Cordifolioside A enhances phagocytic activity of neutrophils through synergistic action with other phytocompounds
Magnoflorine compounds contribute anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory activities
Arabinogalactan polysaccharides activate macrophages via TLR6 signaling
giloy_guduchi_tinospora_cordifolia.who_status: Listed in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API), Volume I, Part I, Monograph No. 34. Recognized by Indian Pharmacopoeia and Indian System of Medicine (ISM). No dedicated WHO monograph identified, though acknowledged in WHO traditional medicine frameworks.

latest_research.title: Efficacy and Safety of Shatavari Root Extract for the Management of Menopausal Symptoms: A Double-Blind, Multicenter, Randomized Controlled Trial
latest_research.finding: Multicenter RCT demonstrated Shatavari root extract was effective and safe for managing menopausal symptoms including hot flashes, night sweats, and mood disturbances.

latest_research.title: Efficacy and Safety of Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus) Root Extract for Perimenopause: Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study
latest_research.finding: 80 participants randomized to Shatavari 300 mg daily or placebo for 8 weeks. Shatavari root extract demonstrated effective and safe natural intervention for perimenopausal symptoms.

latest_research.title: Efficacy and safety of Shatavari root extract (Asparagus racemosus) for menopausal symptoms: a randomized, double-blind, three-arm, placebo-controlled study
latest_research.finding: 135 women aged 45-65 across three arms (Shatavari alone, Shatavari + Ashwagandha, placebo). Both Shatavari alone and the combination were effective; combination showed additive benefits for managing menopausal symptoms and overall health.

latest_research.title: Effects of Shatavari Root Extract on Sexual Wellness in Women: Prospective, Randomized, Double-Blind, Three-Arm, Parallel-Group, Placebo-Controlled Study
latest_research.finding: Standardized Shatavari root extract demonstrated safe and effective improvement in women's sexual health outcomes, with additive effects when combined with Ashwagandha.

latest_research.title: Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus): A Promising Ally for Fertility
latest_research.finding: Review consolidating evidence that Shatavari enhances fertility rates and improves breast milk quality and quantity, supporting its traditional use in postpartum care.

safety_updates: Clinical trials report favorable safety profile at doses of 300-500 mg daily for up to 8 weeks
Mild gastrointestinal complaints (loose stools, nausea) are the most common adverse effects, typically transient and dose-dependent
Phytoestrogenic properties can interfere with estrogen-based medications and hormone replacement therapy (HRT)
Contraindicated in hormone-sensitive conditions: certain cancers (breast, ovarian, uterine), endometriosis, uterine fibroids
May reduce effectiveness of hormonal birth control pills by altering hormone levels or drug absorption
Animal reproductive toxicity studies show no teratogenic effects at therapeutic doses, but rigorous human data still lacking
Mild adverse events in clinical trials: loose stools, dizziness, nausea, headache - all resolving on discontinuation
mechanisms: Phytoestrogenic activity via steroidal saponins (Shatavarins I-IV) binding estrogen receptor alpha (ERalpha), modulating gonadotropin levels
Immunomodulation: Shatavarins stimulate immune cell proliferation and IgG secretion in dose-dependent manner
Th1/Th2 cytokine balance modulation: stimulates IL-12 production while inhibiting IL-6
Shatavarin I blocks oxytocin-induced uterine contractions (in vitro and in vivo) via glycoside-mediated competitive antagonism
Antioxidant activity through polyphenol and flavonoid content scavenging reactive oxygen species
Galactogogue effect attributed to increased prolactin levels mediated by steroidal saponins
shatavari_asparagus_racemosus.who_status: Acknowledged by WHO in medicinal plant monographs, with encouragement for further phytochemical and pharmacological investigation. Listed in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India. Referenced in British Herbal Pharmacopoeia.

latest_research.title: Neem (Azadirachta indica): A Miracle Herb; Panacea for All Ailments
latest_research.finding: Comprehensive review covering neem's applications across pharmaceuticals, agriculture, cosmetics, and fuel production, with focus on broad-spectrum antimicrobial, anticancer, and anti-diabetic properties.

latest_research.title: Predictive modelling and ranking: Azadirachta indica compounds through indices and multi-criteria decision-making techniques
latest_research.finding: Computational study using molecular descriptor indices to rank neem bioactive compounds for drug discovery prioritization, identifying azadirachtin, nimbin, and gedunin as top candidates.

latest_research.title: A systematic review of neem flower (Azadirachta indica)
latest_research.finding: Systematic review demonstrating neem flower extracts improve insulin sensitivity and lower blood sugar levels, with potential as complementary anti-diabetic agents.

latest_research.title: The Antimicrobial Potential of the Neem Tree Azadirachta indica
latest_research.finding: Comprehensive review of antimicrobial activities across dentistry, food safety, bacteriology, mycology, virology, and parasitology. Nimbins demonstrated activity against four dengue virus strains.

latest_research.title: Traditional to modern perspectives on Neem: A gateway to bioactive compounds, sustainable agrochemicals and industrial applications
latest_research.finding: Azadirachta indica leaf extract significantly reduced histological changes and prevented increases in liver enzyme markers in antitubercular drug-induced hepatotoxicity models.

latest_research.title: Phytochemical Profiling, Pharmacokinetics, and Antimicrobial Activity of Azadirachta indica Leaf Extracts: In Silico and In Vitro Evaluations
latest_research.finding: Beta-d-Mannofuranoside identified as a promising antibacterial agent from neem through combined in-silico and in-vitro approaches.

safety_updates: Non-aqueous extracts are most toxic neem products (ESD: 0.002-12.5 mcg/kg bw/day); aqueous extracts safer (ESD: 0.3 mg/kg bw/day)
Prolonged use may cause renal dysfunction, decreased arterial blood pressure, and hypoglycemic responses
Reversible anti-fertility effects on both male and female mammals documented upon sub-acute or chronic exposure
Drug interaction (MODERATE): potentiates hypoglycemic agents - may cause dangerously low blood sugar
Drug interaction (MODERATE): may alter lithium levels requiring dose adjustment
Drug interaction (MODERATE): may interfere with immunosuppressant medications - contraindicated for organ transplant recipients
Insufficient long-term safety data in humans - need for more funded toxicology research emphasized in 2025 bibliometric analysis
Neem oil ingestion in children has been associated with serious adverse events including toxic encephalopathy
mechanisms: Azadirachtin blocks TNF-induced NF-kB activation by binding to TNFR1 at the TNF binding site, preventing TNF binding and downstream signaling
Inhibits IkBalpha phosphorylation and degradation, blocking RelA (p65) nuclear translocation
Reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1beta, TLR4, and NF-kB in dose-dependent manner
Nimbolide and azadirachtin show concentration-dependent free radical scavenging and reductive potential
Prevents procarcinogen activation and oxidative DNA damage; upregulates antioxidant and carcinogen detoxification enzymes
Synergistic activity with existing antibiotics against multidrug-resistant bacterial species
Gedunin acts as HSP90 inhibitor, disrupting protein folding in cancer cells
neem_azadirachta_indica.who_status: Recognized in WHO's monographs on selected medicinal plants. Neem-derived pesticide (azadirachtin) evaluated by WHO/FAO Joint Meeting on Pesticide Residues. Listed in Indian Pharmacopoeia and Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India.

latest_research.title: Terminalia arjuna, a Cardioprotective Herbal Medicine - Relevancy in the Modern Era of Pharmaceuticals and Green Nanomedicine
latest_research.finding: Review examining T. arjuna's pleiotropic cardiovascular effects including anti-atherogenic, hypotensive, inotropic, anti-inflammatory, anti-thrombotic and antioxidant actions, with exploration of nano-formulation approaches for improved bioavailability.

latest_research.title: Terminalia arjuna: An overview of its magical properties
latest_research.finding: Comprehensive overview documenting cardiovascular properties attributed to flavonoids, polyphenols, triterpenoids, tannins, glycosides, and minerals. Highlighted need for more rigorous clinical trials.

latest_research.title: Cardioprotective effects of arjunolic acid in LPS-stimulated H9C2 and C2C12 myotubes via the MyD88-dependent TLR4 signaling pathway
latest_research.finding: Demonstrated arjunolic acid exerts cardioprotection by inhibiting MyD88-dependent TLR4 signaling, reducing LPS-induced cardiac inflammation and oxidative stress in cellular models.

latest_research.title: Nutritional Composition, Phytochemical Profile, Extraction Methods of Bioactive Components, and Health Benefits of Terminalia Arjuna Bark
latest_research.finding: Detailed phytochemical profiling of T. arjuna bark identifying optimal extraction methods for maximizing yield of cardioprotective triterpenoids and polyphenols.

latest_research.title: Clinical efficacy of water extract of stem bark of T. arjuna in patients of chronic heart failure: double-blind RCT
latest_research.finding: When added to standard pharmacotherapy in chronic heart failure for 12 weeks, Arjuna extract showed no significant change in LVEF but improved functional capacity, antioxidant reserves, and symptom-related quality of life. (Most recent large RCT available)

safety_updates: No serious side effects reported with arjuna therapy in clinical studies; long-term safety data still limited
Adverse reactions similar to placebo: constipation, headache, abdominal discomfort, body ache
Drug interaction WARNING: may potentiate anticoagulant effects of warfarin due to inherent antiplatelet and anticoagulant properties similar to aspirin
Inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2D6, and CYP2C9 enzymes in human liver microsomes in vitro - caution with drugs metabolized by these enzymes
In vivo pharmacokinetic study showed aqueous extract did not significantly alter pharmacokinetic parameters of probe substrates, suggesting in vitro findings may not fully translate
High doses in animal studies associated with hepatotoxicity and hypothyroidism in rats
Co-administration with statins, calcium channel blockers, and other CYP3A4 substrates requires medical supervision
mechanisms: Arjunolic acid (pentacyclic triterpenoid saponin) is the primary cardioprotective compound, inhibiting thrombin-induced platelet aggregation (IC50: 0.048 mM, more potent than aspirin at 0.088 mM)
Prevents doxorubicin-induced cardiac apoptosis by blocking JNK-p38 and p53 signaling pathways
Reverses cardiac fibrosis by inhibiting non-canonical TGF-beta signaling via TAK1 phosphorylation blockade, reducing p38 MAPK and NF-kB p65 activation
Boosts endogenous antioxidant defense: increases catalase, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione S-transferase activity
Anti-inflammatory cytokine rebalancing: decreases pro-inflammatory and increases anti-inflammatory cytokines in cardiac tissue
Cardioprotection via MyD88-dependent TLR4 signaling pathway inhibition (2023 discovery)
Positive inotropic effect enhancing myocardial contractility without increasing heart rate
arjuna_terminalia_arjuna.who_status: No dedicated WHO monograph identified. Listed in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India. Recognized in Indian traditional medicine systems (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani). Included in Indian Pharmacopoeia for cardiovascular indications.

latest_research.title: Systematic Review of Shilajit: Clinical Efficacy and Safety
latest_research.finding: PRISMA-guided systematic review of 15 clinical studies (1,254 participants) across chronic fatigue syndrome, high-altitude sickness, cognitive decline, and infertility. Generally mild adverse events (GI discomfort, headache); no serious adverse events reported.

latest_research.title: Shilajit extract preserves bone mineral density in postmenopausal women with osteopenia
latest_research.finding: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial demonstrated Shilajit extract reduced oxidative stress, inflammation, and bone loss in a dose-dependent manner to preserve BMD in postmenopausal women with osteopenia.

latest_research.title: Pre-clinical Evaluation of Shilajit in Cancer: A Systematic Review
latest_research.finding: Systematic review found promising preclinical anticancer evidence but no randomized controlled clinical trials or human studies evaluating Shilajit as a primary anticancer therapy.

latest_research.title: Unlocking the potential of Shilajit in Vascular Dementia - pathology and management
latest_research.finding: Review exploring Shilajit's neuroprotective potential in vascular dementia via cAMP/NO signaling and anti-inflammatory pathways, with fulvic acid blocking tau self-aggregation relevant to Alzheimer's research.

latest_research.title: Shilajit as a Neuroprotective Agent Against Amyloid Beta-induced Cytotoxicity and Inflammation
latest_research.finding: Demonstrated Shilajit's protective effects against amyloid-beta induced neurotoxicity and neuroinflammation in cellular models, supporting potential for neurodegenerative disease applications.

latest_research.title: Effects of oral Shilajit tablets on sexual function and sexual quality of life in reproductive-aged women
latest_research.finding: Triple-blind randomized clinical trial showed significant improvement in sexual function and sexual quality of life in reproductive-aged women following Shilajit supplementation.

latest_research.title: Chemical Analysis of Native Himalayan Shilajit: An Evaluation of an Ayurvedic Formulation
latest_research.finding: ACS Omega publication providing detailed chemical characterization of Himalayan Shilajit identifying dibenzo-alpha-pyrones, fulvic acids, humic acids, trace minerals, and heavy metal profiles.

safety_updates: Processed Shilajit possibly safe at 500 mg daily for up to 48 weeks or 2 g daily for 45 days based on clinical evidence
Adverse events generally mild and transient: gastrointestinal discomfort, headache - no serious adverse events in systematic review of 15 studies
CRITICAL: Raw, unpurified Shilajit may contain arsenic, lead, mercury, and other toxic heavy metals (~65 heavy metals identified including Cu, Al, Pb, As, Cd, Hg)
Thallium contamination identified in some Shilajit supplements (2025 PMC study) - potential risk from unregulated products
Drug interaction: may potentiate hypoglycemic agents causing dangerously low blood sugar
Drug interaction: may interfere with anticoagulants (warfarin) increasing bleeding risk
Drug interaction: may potentiate blood pressure medications causing excessive hypotension
Drug interaction: may affect thyroid medication efficacy
Fulvic acid can bind metals and influence iron uptake - separate dosing from iron supplements by 2-3 hours
Contraindicated in hemochromatosis and individuals prone to kidney stones due to mineral content
Not monitored by FDA for quality or purity - third-party testing (USP, NSF) recommended
mechanisms: Fulvic acid and dibenzo-alpha-pyrones (DBPs) act as electron shuttles in mitochondria, accelerating electron transport at Complex I and Complex III for enhanced ATP production
DBPs function as mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, working in tandem with CoQ10 in the electron transport chain
Fulvic acid chelates minerals enhancing bioavailability and facilitating transport across cell membranes
Fulvic acid blocks tau protein self-aggregation, relevant to Alzheimer's disease pathology
Modulates hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis to attenuate chronic fatigue syndrome symptoms
Preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) and stabilizes complex enzyme activities preventing mitochondrial dysfunction
Reverses mitochondrial oxidative stress: normalizes NO concentration, lipid peroxidation, SOD, and catalase activities
Neuroprotection via cAMP/NO signaling pathway modulation and anti-neuroinflammatory activity
shilajit_mineral_pitch.who_status: No dedicated WHO monograph. Referenced in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India as Shilajatu. USP (United States Pharmacopeia) standards referenced for quality testing. Classified as Rasayana (rejuvenative) in classical Ayurvedic texts including Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita.
